title: Neurobiology of Mental Illness: Neural Circuitry of Depression, Anxiety, & Schizophrenia
description: Deconstruct psychiatric pathophysiology: monoamine and BDNF models of depression, prefrontal-amygdala decoupling in anxiety, and dopamine/NMDA models of schizophrenia.

slides.title: Major Depressive Disorder: Beyond the Monoamine Hypothesis 🌧️
slides.content:
# Re-evaluating the Chemical Imbalance Theory

* **The Classic Monoamine Hypothesis**: Proposed in the 1960s; argued that depression stems from a simple deficiency of serotonin (5-HT) or norepinephrine (NE).
* **The Fatal Therapeutic Lag Paradox**: SSRIs elevate synaptic serotonin within *hours*, yet clinical therapeutic improvement requires **3 to 6 weeks** of treatment! Why?

### The Neurogenic & Synaptogenic Hypothesis:
* Depression is characterized by decreased **Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF)**, impaired neurogenesis, and synaptic loss in the hippocampus and PFC.
* Chronic SSRI administration stimulates intracellular cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling cascades that boost BDNF transcription and restore hippocampal neurogenesis over several weeks.
* **Ketamine Revolution**: Low-dose sub-anesthetic infusions of **Ketamine** (an NMDA receptor antagonist) trigger a rapid glutamate surge, activating AMPA and mTOR pathways to stimulate new dendritic spine synaptogenesis within **hours**, relieving treatment-resistant depression rapidly!

quizData.question: What pharmacological paradox challenged the simplistic monoamine hypothesis of depression?

options.text: Antidepressants raise synaptic serotonin levels within hours, yet clinical symptom relief takes several weeks
Serotonin cannot cross the blood-brain barrier under any circumstances
Patients with depression have higher serotonin than healthy controls

quizData.explanation: The therapeutic lag between immediate monoamine reuptake inhibition and delayed clinical response prompted neurotrophic and synaptic plasticity models.

slides.title: Schizophrenia: Dopamine & Glutamate Hypotheses 🧩
slides.content:
## Neural Circuitry of Psychosis

Schizophrenia affects ~1% of the global population, presenting with positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), negative symptoms (avolition, flat affect), and cognitive deficits.

### 1. The Dopamine Hypothesis (Dual Pathway Model):
* **Mesolimbic Pathway (Hyperactivity)**: Excessive D2 dopamine stimulation in the ventral striatum drives **positive symptoms** (hallucinations/delusions). All effective antipsychotics block D2 receptors.
* **Mesocortical Pathway (Hypoactivity)**: Deficient D1 dopamine signaling in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex underlies **negative and cognitive symptoms**.

### 2. The NMDA Receptor Hypofunction Model:
* Anesthetic drugs like **PCP (phencyclidine)** and **ketamine** block NMDA receptors in healthy humans, producing both positive AND negative/cognitive symptoms indistinguishable from schizophrenia.
* Post-mortem studies show hypofunction of NMDA receptors on parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons in the cortex, causing cortical disinhibition and dysregulated gamma oscillations.

quizData.question: Which dopaminergic pathway is characterized by hyperactivity that drives positive psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and delusions) in schizophrenia?

options.text: Mesolimbic pathway projecting to the ventral striatum

quizData.explanation: Mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia drives positive symptoms (hallucinations/delusions), which are treated by D2 receptor antagonists.
